about: The Prism onboarding course, declared as data. build.mjs writes every page from this file alone, then the content standard (prism/content-standard/1) enriches and measures them. Change this file, not the pages.
title: Prism onboarding course
provenance: Written from [the Prism docs](https://uor.foundation/docs) and [Prism-DevRel](https://afflom.github.io/prism-devrel/). The Calculator commands were run with prism-code 0.9.5 on 2026-11-18. The ticket price and door lock prompts were checked with the Prism-DevRel builder. Lean proofs and `just vv` were not run for the ticket and door examples. The quiz grader's 8 properties were proved by Lean.

pages.title: Prism onboarding course
pages.summary: Learn what Prism proves, run a sample app, write your own app and put it online.
pages.lead: This course takes you from never having heard of Prism to a verified app of your own. Take the modules in order. Each one ends with a short quiz.

figure.title: The course, in order
figure.caption: Six modules and a reference page. Each module builds on the one before it.

head: Module
You will be able to
Time
rows: Say what Prism proves and what it only tests
Follow one sentence to a sealed, checked app file
Inspect, run, check, push and pull the Calculator app
Write a `prism/prompt/1` prompt and read the builder's verdict
Choose a decision table, a policy decision or a state machine
Know what the builder writes and put it on GitHub Pages
Look up a term or a command

blocks.p: Every quiz answer goes to [the Prism course quiz app](../). It is a Prism app built from this course. Lean proved that it never marks a wrong answer right.
The app runs in your browser. A request is the question number and your option, such as `8 a`. It answers `correct` or `incorrect`.
Prism has two front doors. Both share one core: the `app` member of a prompt is the same `prism/spec/1` spec an agent drafts.

head: Agent path
Prompt path
rows: One sentence to your coding agent
`npx prism-code@latest setup` (MCP servers and a skill)
A proved `.holo` app file on your machine
A whole repository: every facet, tests and a site

list: Node.js 22 or later. Modules 3 and 4 run on any laptop.
No account is needed until module 6. To ship, you need git, the `gh` CLI and a GitHub account.
Lean proofs run on the hosted verifier, or on your machine in the SDK image (Docker, about 5.5 GB).

pages.title: Why Prism
pages.summary: What Prism proves for every request, what it only tests, and which apps it fits.
pages.lead: Tests check the cases someone thought of. With Prism you state what your app must never do and must always do. Lean then proves each statement for every possible request.

figure.title: What Prism proves and what it tests
figure.caption: Left, three parts of an app description. Right, what each becomes. Only a property becomes a theorem.

blocks.p: The app ships as one sealed file. Anyone can check that file before they run it.

blocks.h2: Proved and tested are different claims

blocks.p: **Proved** means the Lean kernel checked a property for every request. **Tested** means the examples replayed correctly.
Rules, examples and the reading of requests are tested, not proved. Nothing proves that your rules are the right rules. That judgment stays with you.

head: Part of the app
Proved or tested
How it is checked
rows: A theorem the Lean kernel checks for every request
The examples, and the properties that constrain it
Replayed byte for byte as an acceptance vector
Its BLAKE3 fingerprint is recomputed on load

blocks.p: Use Prism when a wrong answer is costly. Good first apps are approvals, eligibility, limits, access rules, and checks an agent relies on.
Today the guided path builds decision apps within these limits:

head: Part
Limit today
rows: One line of up to 8 fields, separated by spaces
A whole number, or a choice of 2 to 32 words
One of a fixed set of outcomes, plus the reserved `invalid`
Up to 24, tried in order; the first match decides
Compare a field with a value or another field: `is`, `is not`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`

blocks.p: **Conditions do no arithmetic.** A leap year app cannot test whether a year divides by 4. Pass the result in as a field instead, such as `divisible-by-4: yes or no`.

quiz.q: A property says the app never answers full when age is below 16. What does Lean check?
quiz.why: Each property becomes a theorem proved for every request, not a sample.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good first Prism app?
quiz.why: The guided path is built for decision apps where a wrong answer is costly.

quiz.q: A leap year app must know whether a year divides by 4. How do you model that?
options: Add a field such as divisible-by-4: yes or no
quiz.why: Conditions cannot do arithmetic, so the caller supplies the result as a field.

pages.title: How it works
pages.summary: How one sentence becomes a proved, sealed app file, and what is checked before it runs.
pages.lead: One description, proved by Lean, produces the program. This page follows it from a sentence to a running app.

figure.title: From a sentence to a running app
figure.caption: You write the first two steps. Prism writes the next three. Anyone who receives the file runs the last two.

dl: Sentence
Describe what the app decides. On the agent path, ask something like “Build me a Prism app that decides whether a payment is approved.”
Spec
Purpose, fields, outcomes, ordered rules, properties and examples. Read the properties most carefully: they are the only part that is proved.
LexLean model
Prism writes the spec as a model in LexLean. The proof and the program both come from it. So a proof about the model is a proof about what runs.
Proofs and program
Each property becomes a theorem the Lean kernel checks. The program is a WebAssembly guest with no imports: no clock, randomness, network or files.
.holo file
One file with the program, the model, its build record, its permissions and a browser view. Its BLAKE3 fingerprint names it.
Verify
Three questions. Are these the sealed bytes? Who signed what? Is that evidence enough to run it here?
Run or share
Run one request, serve the view on a port, or push to a registry. A pull writes nothing until the checks pass.

blocks.p: Before an app runs, Prism works out how much signed evidence it carries. Only signing raises the level. Apps built today are unsigned, so they are P0.

head: Level
Carries
Asked for by
rows: Nothing signed (bytes and examples are still verified)

blocks.p: A policy says which level is enough. To run an unsigned app on purpose, write `{"minimum":"P0"}` to a policy file a reviewer can see.

Until the SDK image is on your machine, proofs run on the hosted verifier at [mcp.uor.foundation](https://mcp.uor.foundation/). It stores the files under `src/` unlisted. Anyone with the draft ID can read them.
**Never put secrets in a model.**

quiz.q: What does the .holo fingerprint protect against?
quiz.why: Loading recomputes the BLAKE3 fingerprint. If one byte changed, the file is refused.

quiz.q: Why does prism-code run refuse the sample app by default?
options: It is P0, and the default policy asks for P2
quiz.why: That is the safety check working. Pass a policy that accepts P0 on purpose.

quiz.q: Which parts of an app are proved, rather than tested?
quiz.why: Only properties are proved. Rules, examples and request reading are tested.

pages.title: Try the sample app
pages.summary: Install prism-code, then look inside, check, run, push and pull its sample app.
pages.lead: The prism-code package ships a small Calculator app. These seven steps use it. Every output below is what prism-code 0.9.5 printed, with long digests shortened.

figure.title: Seven commands on the sample app
figure.caption: Each step uses the same file. Nothing is built; you only read, judge and run it.

blocks.p: The package bundles the sample app. Keep its path in a variable.

blocks.output:
Name:      Calculator
Size:      24801 B
Footer:    8408e089...21ba (BLAKE3 of the body)
Model:
  Function:     calculate
  Vectors:      22
  Limits:       request 52 B, response 27 B, guest allocation 65536 B
World:
  Imports:         none
  Purity:          pure: no clock, random, socket or filesystem import
Attestations:
  none
Verification:
  Footer:            ok
  Labels:            ok
  Cross-references:  ok

blocks.p: Nothing runs. `Imports: none` means the app cannot reach a clock, randomness, the network or files.

blocks.output: 22 of 22 vectors passed (holo, Calculator, identities verified)

blocks.p: Each example is compared byte for byte. Exit code 0 means all of them passed.

blocks.output:
FAILED  P0 unverified  policy default requires P2 or above
Reasons:
  provenance.statement (Verification, withholds P1)
  proof.statement (ProofMismatch, withholds P2)
  replay.statement (Replay, withholds P3)
  policy.level (PP5601, Verification, policy rule)
    The level is P0; the policy requires P2 or above.
exit=1

blocks.p: This is the safety check working. The bytes are fine, but nothing is signed.

blocks.code:
echo '{"minimum":"P0"}' > policy.json
npx prism-code check $H --policy policy.json --json

blocks.p: `--allow-unverified` does the same, but warns on every start. A policy file is better, because a reviewer can see it.
A request is tab-separated: version, operation, then the operands.

blocks.code:
npx prism-code run $H "$(printf '1\tadd\t20\t22')" --policy policy.json --rm
npx prism-code run $H "$(printf '1\tdivide\t1\t0')" --policy policy.json --rm; echo " exit=$?"
npx prism-code run $H "$(printf '1\tmod\t1\t2')" --policy policy.json --rm

blocks.output:
1	ok	42
1	error	division-by-zero exit=0
1	error	unknown-operation

blocks.p: The operations are `add`, `subtract`, `multiply` and `divide`. An error answer is still a successful run, so the exit code is 0. `--rm` keeps no run record.

blocks.code:
npx prism-code push $H dir://./store:1.0
npx prism-code pull dir://./store:1.0 pulled.holo
cmp $H pulled.holo && echo identical

blocks.output:
1.0: digest: sha256:208bb91c...b5e4 size: 968
fingerprint: blake3:8408e089...21ba
Verdict: P0, policy pull-default requires P0
Status: Verified and wrote pulled.holo
identical

blocks.p: `pull` accepts P0, while `run` and `check` ask for P2. A failed check writes nothing.

head: Command
rows: no verdict: treat it as a failure
a mismatch, or an altered file

quiz.q: What does prism-code inspect do to the app?
quiz.why: inspect prints the sections, digests, model and world. Nothing runs.

quiz.q: A divide by zero answers 1 error division-by-zero. What is the exit code?
quiz.why: An error answer is still a successful run.

quiz.q: prism-code check exits 2. What does that mean?
options: No verdict: treat it as a failure
quiz.why: 0 passed, 1 failed, 2 means no verdict was reached.

pages.title: Your first app
pages.summary: Write one prompt for a ticket price app, see the builder refuse a broken rule, then build it.
pages.lead: A prompt is one JSON document. Its `app` member is the spec, and the rest is optional. This page writes a prompt for a cinema ticket price, then checks it.

figure.title: How the builder judges a prompt
figure.caption: The builder writes nothing until the examples agree and every property holds for all 242 possible requests.

head: `app` member
What to write
In the example
rows: What the app decides, in one sentence
the price band of one cinema ticket
A request is these values in order, separated by spaces
`when` and `then`, in order; the first match decides
The answer when no rule matches
no child or senior pays full; under-3s are free
Requests and their answers; each becomes an acceptance vector
What the app does not decide
a member under 3 still goes free

blocks.p: Save it as `ticket.prompt.json`. The builder accepted it: 3 properties, 29 acceptance vectors and 82 files.
This runs the same first-match rules and the same check of every request as the builder, in your browser. Switch rules off to see what breaks.

list: Switch off REQ-003. What does the builder refuse, and why?
Switch it back on, then switch off REQ-001. Which example breaks first?
Type `121 no`, then `07 no`. Why is each one `invalid`?

blocks.h2: Check it on the command line

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/afflom/prism-devrel.git && cd prism-devrel
node builder/cli.mjs check ticket.prompt.json
node builder/cli.mjs build ticket.prompt.json --out my-app

blocks.output:
Ticket price: Decision table (OMG DMN 1.5, hit policy FIRST), 82 files, 29 acceptance vectors
TP-01: The app never answers full when age is below 16
TP-02: The app never answers full when age is at least 65
TP-03: The app always answers free when age is below 3
...

blocks.p: With the senior rule removed, the real builder refused the prompt and named the request that breaks it:

blocks.output:
refused: INV-002 does not hold. The request `65 no` meets "age is at least 65",
and the rules answer full (otherwise). Change a rule, or restate the property.
exit=2

blocks.p: Open [the builder at /start](https://afflom.github.io/prism-devrel/start/). Pick an example, edit the prompt and build the app. It runs in the page and sends nothing anywhere.

quiz.q: Two rules match 10 yes: REQ-002 (age below 16) and REQ-004 (member). Which decides?
quiz.why: Rules are tried in order, and the first match decides (DMN hit policy FIRST).

quiz.q: You remove the senior rule. What does the builder do?
options: Refuses, and names 65 no as the request that breaks INV-002
quiz.why: A broken property comes back with a counterexample, before anything is written.
maybe is not a value of the member field, so the request is malformed.

pages.title: Choose a pattern
pages.summary: Pick one of three patterns for your app, then write a state machine.
pages.lead: Set `pattern` in the prompt to choose how the answer is read. Each pattern follows a published standard, and the builder checks the prompt against it.

figure.title: Patterns in the example gallery
figure.caption: The 34 example prompts on Prism-DevRel, counted by pattern. Most apps are decision tables.

head: `pattern`
Pick it when
Standard
Guide
rows: The answer is one of your outcomes, chosen by ordered rules
The answer is permit, deny, not-applicable or indeterminate
The answer is the next state, from the current state and an event

blocks.p: The state travels in the request, so the app keeps nothing between requests. Fill in the `machine` member:

list: `state` is the field that holds the current state.
`initial` is the state a run starts in.
`final` lists the states a run never leaves.
The outcomes must be exactly the values of the state field.

blocks.p: Here is a door lock, summarized from a prompt the builder accepted:

blocks.code:
"pattern": "stateMachine",
"machine": {"state": "state", "initial": "closed", "final": ["retired"]},
fields:  state = closed | open | locked | retired
         event = push | shut | lock | unlock | retire
rules (first match wins):
  state is retired                  -> retired
  event is retire                   -> retired
  state is closed and event is push -> open
  state is closed and event is lock -> locked
  state is open and event is shut   -> closed
  state is locked and event unlock  -> closed
  state is open                     -> open
  state is locked                   -> locked
  otherwise                         -> closed
properties:
  never locked when state is open
  never open when state is locked and event is push

blocks.p: Check it the same way as any prompt:

blocks.output:
Door lock: State machine (OMG UML 2.5.1 behavioral state machine), 82 files, 30 acceptance vectors
machine: 4 states from closed; reachable closed, open, locked, retired; final retired; derived INV-003
DL-01: The app never answers locked when state is open
DL-02: The app never answers open when state is locked and event is push
DL-03: The app always answers retired when state is retired
...

blocks.p: The builder found which states can be reached. From `final`, it added INV-003: a retired lock stays retired.

quiz.q: The answers must be exactly permit, deny, not-applicable and indeterminate. Which pattern?
Where does a state machine app keep its state between requests?
quiz.why: The state travels in the request, so the app keeps nothing between requests.

quiz.q: What does the builder prove in addition for a state machine?
options: A final state is never left, and no run leaves the reachable states
quiz.why: Those theorems come from machine.final and machine.initial.

pages.title: Ship your app
pages.summary: See what the builder writes from your prompt, then put the app on GitHub Pages.
pages.lead: A Prism app is one model with several facets, such as architecture, security and quality. Every facet but behavior follows from the behavior by fixed rules.

figure.title: From a prompt to a live site
figure.caption: You do the first four steps. The repository's Pages workflow does the last two on every push.

blocks.p: Leave the optional prompt members out and you still get every facet, with defaults. Add them to describe your real system.

head: Prompt member
Facet
Records
Checked against
rows: The model, a theorem per property, acceptance vectors
An OPM view; UML component, sequence and state views
A feature per rule and property, a journey per stakeholder
Assets, STRIDE threats, risks, controls with evidence
An obligation per standard, each naming its evidence

blocks.p: Set `repository` in the prompt to `OWNER/prism-NAME`, where NAME is `app.name`. Build the zip, then run:

blocks.code:
gh repo create OWNER/prism-NAME --template UOR-Foundation/template --public
gh api -X POST repos/OWNER/prism-NAME/pages -f build_type=workflow
git -c core.autocrlf=false clone https://github.com/OWNER/prism-NAME.git
cd prism-NAME
git rm -q app/src/Contract.lex.tex crates/conformance/tests/contract.rs features/suites/contract.feature
unzip -o ../prism-NAME.zip
git add -A && git commit -m "Build the app from its prompt" && git push

blocks.p: The push starts the Pages workflow. It runs the gate, `just vv`, which proves the app with the Lean kernel. Then it publishes the site.
To run the same gate first, follow [How to verify an app](https://afflom.github.io/prism-devrel/guides/verify/).

blocks.h2: House rules of a template repository

list: The model is the single source. Change the prompt, not the generated files.
`just vv` is the whole acceptance boundary. It runs in the SDK image that `prismpm.lock` pins.
A gate counts as evidence only after a planted defect shows it can fail.
Nothing is stubbed or hidden behind a flag.

quiz.q: Which prompt member becomes the security and threat model facet?
quiz.why: threats become STRIDE threats, risks and controls (ISO/IEC 27005 and 27034).

quiz.q: What is the complete acceptance gate of a template repository?
options: just vv, in the SDK image that prismpm.lock pins
quiz.why: just vv is the whole acceptance boundary. The Pages workflow runs it too.

quiz.q: You want to change a generated facet file. What should you do?
options: Change the prompt and build again
quiz.why: The prompt is the single source. Every file is written from it the same way each time.

pages.title: Reference
pages.summary: Terms, commands and exit codes from the course, on one page.
pages.lead: Look up a term or a command. Nothing here needs to be read in order.

figure.title: Signed statements at each evidence level
figure.caption: Each level adds one signed statement to the one before it. P0 carries none.

dl: Rule
A `when` and `then` line. Rules are tried in order, and the first match decides. Tested, not proved.
Example
A request with its exact expected answer. It becomes an acceptance vector carried in the app.
World
What the program may use. Today that is `hologram:guest/core-wasm@1`, which allows nothing.
Verdict
The result of a policy check: the level, pass or fail, and every reason (`prism/verdict/1`).
Hosted verifier
The service at mcp.uor.foundation. It checks and proves models when the SDK image is not on your machine.
`just vv`
The complete acceptance gate of a template repository, run in the pinned SDK image.

blocks.p: Words marked on any page, such as property and policy, are defined at the foot of that page.

blocks.code:
# Set up the agent path (preview first)
npx prism-code@latest setup --dry-run
npx prism-code@latest setup

# Look, replay, judge, run
npx prism-code inspect app.holo
npx prism-code vectors app.holo
npx prism-code check app.holo --policy policy.json [--json]
npx prism-code run app.holo "<request>" --policy policy.json --rm
npx prism-code run app.holo --port 8080 --policy policy.json

# Catch changed answers between builds
npx prism-code record app.holo --output history.json
npx prism-code replay history.json --image new.holo

# Share
npx prism-code push app.holo dir://./store:1.0
npx prism-code pull dir://./store:1.0 pulled.holo

# Prompt path, from a clone of afflom/prism-devrel
node builder/cli.mjs check prompt.json
node builder/cli.mjs build prompt.json --out my-app
node builder/cli.mjs schema
